Lowering their ambitions to the limited goal of stability makes it possible to dampen volatility, achieve tangible progress, and work with the reality of interdependence in more productive ways.
One of the most significant changes underlying the acceptance of strategic stability is China’s growing confidence. When the first Trump administration began pushing for more decoupling, in 2018, many Chinese policymakers and citizens alike worried that escalating tensions with the United States would harm China’s progress and end the prospect of China developing into a stronger and wealthier country. In contemporary China, development is linked to openness: the more international cooperation there is, the faster technological development proceeds. The United States’ embrace of strategic competition challenged this basic premise. The outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic and the war in Ukraine, which further drove countries apart and into blocs, made decision-makers and ordinary citizens worry even more.
But after eight years of on-and-off trade and technology wars with the United States, China’s economic fundamentals have remained stable. Real estate markets are struggling and traditional industries are mired in distress, but high-tech industries have advanced by leaps and bounds and the manufacturing sector, particularly advanced manufacturing, has become stronger. China’s inability to obtain semiconductors from the United States has forced it to strengthen its own chip industry. The mainstream view in China now is that U.S. government restrictions on high-tech sectors have forced China onto a better path toward more self-reliance and innovation, rendering Washington’s containment policies ineffective and ultimately counterproductive.
China’s successes are mounting. In early 2025, the Chinese firm DeepSeek released a large language model that achieved near-parity with U.S. frontier AI models at a fraction of the cost. In April of that year, China successfully retaliated against Trump’s tariffs, forcing Washington back to the negotiating table. In those negotiations and later talks, China’s rare-earth dominance gave the country a chokepoint over U.S. supply chains. These episodes have increased China’s confidence and made its policymakers and strategists less worried about discussing competition as part of China’s relationship with the United States.
Western commentators often believe that a confident China will become more assertive. The opposite is true. When China’s leaders believe that they can manage their external environment and that the country’s core interests and development prospects are not threatened, they are more willing to show restraint, engage in consultation, and focus on solving problems at home. In the 1990s and the first decade of the twenty-first century, for example, as China’s economy grew rapidly, it shelved disputes in the South China Sea with its neighbors. It was only after the Obama administration’s “pivot to Asia,” when Beijing felt that the United States was uniting countries in the region against China, that it adopted a tougher approach to resolving disputes in the South China Sea.
In 2026, a more confident China did not exploit the difficulties that the United States faced in the war with Iran, but instead quietly promoted peace talks behind the scenes. Likewise, now that China is less worried that the United States has either the intention or the ability to block China’s development prospects, it is more willing to accept a bounded competition with the United States. From a position of confidence, Beijing can engage the United States pragmatically on an issue-by-issue basis, looking to find specific policies to manage an inevitable amount of competition.
The fundamental requirement of the new framework of strategic stability is maintaining peace. That requires that the Chinese and U.S. militaries establish more mature measures for crisis avoidance, crisis management, and confidence building. The two sides can reduce the likelihood of conflict at low cost by setting up regularized military-to-military exchanges and fleshing out and expanding existing maritime and air encounter protocols. They can also coordinate on issues related to outer space, such as preventing near-earth-orbit collisions, regulating space traffic, and building trust around their respective strategic intentions. Addressing concerns in more politically sensitive domains, such as nuclear weapons and the military application of artificial intelligence, will require a more gradual approach. Although the Trump administration has shown heightened interest in discussing nuclear arms control with China, Beijing believes that formal negotiations are premature because of the vast disparity between U.S. and Chinese nuclear capabilities.
Progress does not need to be confined to top leaders. More exchanges at all levels between China and the United States are another low-cost way of solidifying a framework of strategic stability. The United States and China could increase opportunities for engagement by easing visa restrictions and reviewing and reducing sanctions, removing entry or exit bans, and limiting other travel restrictions on institutions and citizens, as well as allowing more of the other side’s news media to operate there. Trump could take the opportunity to explicitly remind Chinese students that they are welcome to study in the United States, and Beijing could formulate clearer policies to guide scholars and students about the boundaries of acceptable research in China and guarantee openness, safety, and academic freedom for any scholarship falling outside those boundaries.
Taiwan remains a dangerous flash point that could set back progress toward a relationship of strategic stability. Taiwan is the only issue that could trigger a deliberate military conflict between China and the United States, and pressure is increasing. Continued rule of the island by the more pro-independence Democratic Progressive Party, combined with Beijing’s strong desire to advance national unification and uncertainty about what kind of Taiwan policy the United States is going to pursue, has inflamed tensions on all sides. A new equilibrium can emerge only through an arrangement in which no party is completely satisfied yet each can live with the result.
As long as Beijing believes that cross-strait integration remains achievable, it has no reason to resort to military force. The United States could shift its declared policy to align more closely with Beijing by recognizing Chinese sovereignty over Taiwan or by explicitly opposing Taiwan’s independence, which would reassure Beijing that the prospect of “peaceful reunification” remains viable. This would allow China and the United States to reach a consensus that realizes the U.S. objective of a peaceful resolution to the dispute yet also maintains the ability of the people in Taiwan to preserve their political and social systems. By keeping the prospect of peaceful reunification alive, the core concerns of all three parties can be accommodated as much as possible.
Washington’s decision to pause $14 billion in arms sales to Taiwan, reached during Trump’s May summit with Xi, defused a rapidly escalating flash point in U.S.-Chinese relations. But it presents a new challenge to the nascent framework of strategic stability. Although Beijing certainly welcomed the delay, the pause has also raised expectations for future U.S. policy regarding Taiwan. Should the Trump administration eventually resume arms transfers—an outcome deemed likely by most Washington observers—Beijing will fiercely oppose the move, potentially jeopardizing the strategic stability framework. This scenario represents a concrete and salient threat that both countries must manage in the period ahead.
A relationship of strategic stability is not a concept that one side imposed on the other or that will benefit Beijing but hurt Washington. It is the result of joint efforts by both countries, which makes it a rare opportunity. The next step is to build out this basic framework, breathe life into it, and make it sustainable. The September summit and additional scheduled leaders’ meetings this year offer a timely window of opportunity to make further small steps toward solidifying this baseline of stability. Some believe that this goal is too modest. But if two major powers such as China and the United States can keep fluctuations in the relationship within a manageable range and avoid any kind of war, it would be far more than a modest achievement.
articles.summary: A confident Beijing and a pragmatic Washington can get along.

articles.title: Avoiding the Next Famine
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
ANNA NELSON is Executive Director of the Food Security Leadership Council. A career civil servant at the Departments of State and Defense under three administrations, she served as Deputy Special Envoy for Global Food Security from 2024 to 2025.
CARY FOWLER is President of the Food Security Leadership Council. He served as U.S. Special Envoy for Global Food Security from 2022 to 2025, and he is a 2024 World Food Prize laureate.
In a world of great-power standoffs, climatic tipping points, and technological arms races, global hunger may not seem like a particularly significant problem. Yet last year, a total of 2.1 billion people, or more than a quarter of the planet’s population, experienced food insecurity—meaning they either ran out of food over the course of a year or were forced to reduce the quality or quantity of their diet. Over 260 million faced acute food insecurity, meaning their lives or livelihoods were in immediate danger because they could not get enough to eat. Almost a quarter of all children under the age of five were permanently stunted because of malnourishment and will likely reach lower levels of education, earn less over the course of their lives, and live with more chronic health challenges than properly fed kids. And these startling figures do not reflect the food crises that could be unleashed this year by rising energy and fertilizer prices, decreases in grain exports from Russia and Ukraine, and an intensifying El Niño weather pattern.
Food insecurity is terrible in and of itself. But it also has disastrous political consequences. It inhibits economic growth, heightens the risk of violent conflict, and destabilizes governments. These problems, in turn, create trouble for the whole world. That means countries that are not overwhelmed by food insecurity still have strong, self-interested reasons to tackle it—the United States included.
In fact, a U.S.-led effort to address hunger would do more than create a healthier and more stable planet. Given the waning goodwill toward the United States, Washington needs an agenda through which it can rebuild global confidence in its leadership and demonstrate the value of international cooperation. Addressing global food security could be at the center of such a plan. Different parts of the world, after all, may have different geopolitical ambitions. But almost no government—northern or southern, democratic or autocratic—wants to see so many people go hungry. There may be no better way to rebuild confidence in the liberal world order and in the United States as a committed member of it than for Washington to address this challenge.
It is difficult to overstate just how intertwined food security is with global development, state security, and even international competition. Malnutrition leads to reduced educational attainment, compromised human capital, and lost productivity, costing the world economy $3.5 trillion a year in forgone economic growth and in added health-care costs. Food price spikes can also exacerbate grievances and lead to riots that destabilize governments; anger over hunger, for example, set the conditions for the Arab Spring protests. In rural areas, food insecurity helps armed groups recruit soldiers and causes disputes over scarce land and water resources. And it causes people to migrate to wealthier states.
These reasons are, by themselves, enough for Washington to helm a global campaign to reduce hunger. But so should the fact that leading on global food security means helping shape the future of the world’s entire agricultural system—something China is on a path to do. In 2019, Beijing invested significant capital in securing leadership of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the UN, a role with substantial influence over how governments work together on food-related issues. It is also quickly developing other ways to lead the world on matters of food security. China spends double what the United States spends on public agricultural research and development, and its output of agricultural patents and scientific publications has skyrocketed while U.S. output has stagnated.
Thankfully for American officials, the United States is still well positioned to lead the world when it comes to food security. The United States is among the world’s largest agricultural exporters. It was instrumental in founding the UN architecture dedicated to food security, including the Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Food Program. And for much of these institutions’ history, Washington has been their largest donor. In fact, for decades, the United States’ international development agenda was the most ambitious in the world, and it was backed by a willing public.
The country still has such a public: in early 2026 polling, a strong majority said that the United States should be a moral leader in the world. But a strong majority didn’t believe it was. Perhaps this is because the United States has been walking away from this legacy and this opportunity to lead. In mid-2025, for example, Congress clawed back nearly $8 billion in foreign assistance funds. The United States is now a reluctant international donor and a surly member of key international organizations.
Washington, however, still retains many of the tools needed to combat global hunger. In addition to increasing foreign assistance, it can leverage trade policies, public investment in innovation, and even its impressive data collection systems. Washington, however, will also need to work multilaterally. And to build credibility, it should advance a practical and achievable agenda with clear benefits for all. One overarching goal for collective action should be increasing predictability wherever possible. The global food system is afflicted by uncertainty across many domains—weather, supply chains, labor, trade, and beyond. This wreaks havoc on policymaking, markets, and livelihoods. Being able to better understand these trends and know what tools will be available to manage them could thus do much to shore up food networks and prepare for disasters.
Washington should, for example, work with partners to strengthen the world’s fractured early warning systems and the data that enables them. Early warning of shocks to the food system—such as extreme weather, supply disruptions, economic turbulence—buys critical time for preparation and response. The United States should also spearhead the transition of international emergency food assistance funding away from voluntary, ad hoc contributions to preplanned, multiyear commitments. It should simultaneously encourage more donors to contribute in amounts commensurate with their abilities, starting with itself.
Solving food emergencies requires more than just additional funding. The United States also needs to work to strengthen international norms that protect access to food during conflict. That means making sure humanitarian groups can get into conflict zones, protecting agricultural infrastructure from attacks, and prohibiting the use of starvation as a weapon of war. These concepts have a long-standing basis in international law, but the conflicts in Gaza, Sudan, and Ukraine have demonstrated they need reinforcement. Washington should advance these norms through resolutions and interventions in the UN Security Council and General Assembly and use diplomacy to try to get violators to change their behavior.
Food security diplomacy, however, must extend beyond conflict zones. The United States should forge a broad global commitment to avoid unilateral, reactionary policies to agricultural shocks—such as when a grain exporter suddenly bans external shipments in response to price spikes, leaving international buyers in the lurch. Such policies may be politically attractive for governments that want to show citizens they will keep costs down. But they leave other states worse off and often don’t even work at home. Instead, the United States should promote more international financing options that maintain the flow of traded agricultural commodities during periods of price volatility and that fast-track funding to countries facing shocks.
Finally, the United States should lead a collective action campaign aimed at protecting agricultural systems from a particularly pernicious challenge: agricultural pests and diseases. Pests and diseases destroy up to 40 percent of global crop production each year, pushing down rural incomes, driving up consumer prices, and wasting natural resources. The existing international surveillance and response systems for these ailments are limited in scope. But Washington can build global support for more comprehensive ones.
The world certainly needs better ways of managing food crisis and risk. But it also needs to foster sustainable agricultural productivity growth—or the ability to produce more food with fewer inputs. Such growth is particularly important where populations are rising, as most food consumed is produced domestically. Only certain food commodities can be easily traded across long distances, so international commerce cannot fully solve food and nutritional supply challenges.
The most important step countries can collectively take is to promote innovation. To encourage that process, U.S. officials should start by focusing on international agricultural research centers, such as the World Vegetable Center in Taiwan and the International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center in Mexico (both of which the United States helped found). These facilities have long been an engine for progress in productivity, food security, and natural resource management, particularly in the developing world. For example, over the last few decades, international centers have developed flood-tolerant rice and drought-tolerant corn that have prevented crop failure for millions of poorer smallholder farmers. In fact, according to studies by a variety of economists, research undertaken by these centers offers an impressive return on investment—for every dollar spent, ten dollars are gained in the form of yield increases, lower production costs, lower consumer prices, and other benefits. But like many institutions, these research centers have suffered from mission creep and bureaucratic accretion. To maximize their effectiveness, the United States should build global support for refocusing their strategy, streamlining their operations, and making new investments in them.
The world needs research to keep just ahead of the latest challenges—such as rising temperatures and new strains of old agricultural diseases. But it should also aim higher. Washington thus ought to work with other actors to tackle tough, high-reward problems that have never had the benefit of a truly concerted international effort. This could include, for example, trying to develop high-yielding perennial or nitrogen-fixing grains that would promote healthier landscapes, reduce labor requirements, and need less fertilizer. It might also feature an endeavor to increase photosynthesis efficiency so that plants can produce more from the sunlight they receive. Such inventions would not only change the world, they would also showcase the power of American innovation and deepen Washington’s ties with its partners.
But to enable ambitious research, the United States should take steps to reform the International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture. The agreement was designed to make plant genetic resources, or seeds and tissue, fully and freely available to researchers everywhere. These resources can be used to breed new varieties of crops that are higher yielding, more resilient to climate change, and more nutritious. But the treaty is falling short. Researchers see benefit-sharing provisions as too costly; developing countries see them as offering too little. As a result, fewer researchers seek material that could accelerate innovation, and fewer countries are willing to share it. The United States should thus push everyone to reinterpret the benefit-sharing provisions in a more generous manner. It should also properly fund the Global Crop Diversity Trust’s endowment, which funds the international seed banks that conserve the biological foundation of food crops (particularly since governments, including Washington, are doing an inadequate job of conserving their collections). And if U.S. officials determine that the treaty cannot be saved, they should lead an effort to draft a new one.
Lastly, Washington must do whatever it can to make sure that new agricultural and food technologies are quickly adopted. This will require reforms of the international Codex Alimentarius Commission, which is responsible for developing food safety guidelines that protect consumers and facilitate trade. The commission’s guidelines have significant ramifications for technologies that could strengthen global food security, but the body is slow, underfunded, and controversial. The United States should therefore try to enhance its capacity and legitimacy, including by pushing for increased support to the scientific committees that help set Codex standards.
At a time of rising global competition, there are few issues that can bring the whole world together. Food security is one of them. Almost every government knows that hunger is a problem, and almost all of them at least say they want to address it. If the United States can spearhead a strong effort do so, it could bring the planet together under its leadership.
That does not mean Washington should instrumentalize food aid or other agricultural endeavors. The United States should not echo its 1970s policies around food power, during which officials boasted of altruism while attempting to exert political strength by alternatively deploying and withholding its grain supply. Instead, the United States must emphasize mutual benefit. It must persuade other actors that it is a constructive and reliable partner. Doing so will strengthen its diplomatic relationships and increase stability around the world—inherently advancing U.S. interests.
Rarely do Washington’s strategic imperatives and humanitarian principles align so neatly. It is rarer still for a U.S. foreign policy agenda to clearly reflect what the American people want their country to be: not just strong, but moral. Food security, in other words, is a unique opportunity for the United States. The country cannot afford to waste it.
articles.summary: What Washington can do to stop starvation.

articles.title: How Taiwan Can Win the Strait
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
HOLMES LIAO is Senior Adviser at the Taiwan Space Agency and a former Honorary Chair at the War College of Taiwan’s National Defense University.
DENNIS BLAIR was Commander in Chief of U.S. Pacific Command from 1999 to 2002 and Director of National Intelligence from 2009 to 2010.
Separated from China by a roughly 100-mile-wide strait, Taiwan relies on its navy as the first line of defense against a potential invasion. It must be able to prevent an assault by a Chinese force carried across the Taiwan Strait in large amphibious ships. Taiwan has traditionally favored large ships such as destroyers and frigates to form the core of its fleet, both as visible symbols of state power and as tools for signaling resolve in the face of Chinese coercion, and Taiwan’s current shipbuilding plans include replacing an aging surface fleet with large and expensive new ships.
Yet large surface ships are vulnerable in the narrow waters of the Taiwan Strait—a problem compounded by advances in technology that are making them easier to detect, track, and attack. China has invested in cutting-edge intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (collectively known as ISR), as well as electronic warfare systems, drones, and missiles. Taiwan’s large surface ships are now a liability. But Taiwan has an advantage: these same technologies make China’s large amphibious ships more vulnerable in restricted waters, and those ships cannot be replaced by smaller, stealthier alternatives. Taipei can take advantage of this mismatch by replacing its destroyers and frigates with a greater number of smaller surface combatants that are more likely to survive an initial wave of Chinese strikes and remain capable of attacking a Chinese invasion fleet.
The Taiwanese navy is planning to invest heavily in large surface combatants, including a new 7,000-ton warship and as many as 12 3,000-ton light frigates. These large ships are impediments to the radical transformation of the Taiwanese navy that the Chinese threat requires. Building ships of this size with stealth features and defense systems to survive a battle in the Taiwan Strait would be prohibitively costly; without these features, they would be too vulnerable to play a major role in the navy’s primary wartime mission of denying a Chinese invasion force the use of the Taiwan Strait. Efforts elsewhere to build similarly capable ships have proved costly and difficult. The U.S. Navy’s Constellation-class frigate program, for example, budgeted roughly $1 billion per ship; the cost eventually rose to about $1.5 billion each before the Constellation program was canceled, and even at that price the ships lacked the capabilities needed to fight an advanced adversary in restricted waters. In comparison, the spending on Taiwan’s entire shipbuilding program is projected to be $1.5 billion annually.
Rather than spend resources on large ships, Taipei should build stealthy corvettes weighing between 700 and 1,000 tons, armed with missiles and drones, that are harder to detect and target but can retain enough firepower to attack Chinese ships crossing the strait. Combined with current plans to build shore-based mobile launchers, aircraft armed with antiship missiles, and eight submarines, Taiwan can create a dispersed and hard-to-destroy defense system that can withstand Chinese attacks and repel a potential amphibious assault.
Large ships may be potent signals of national power, but they are relatively easy to target and politically costly to lose. When ships are fighting in narrow waterways under heavy surveillance, visibility quickly becomes a deadly liability. The sinking of a large ship can also have consequences beyond an immediate military setback. A highly visible and costly loss may make political and military leaders more cautious about risking additional warships as conflict continues.
Major naval engagements over more than the last four decades suggest that any navy expecting to fight near an enemy’s coast should be wary of building its force structure around expensive, irreplaceable hulls. The 1982 Falklands War between Argentina and the United Kingdom, for example, showed how a single successful strike on a warship can constrain an entire surface fleet. Argentina entered the Falklands conflict with powerful ships, including the cruiser General Belgrano and the aircraft carrier Veinticinco de Mayo. But after a British submarine sank the Belgrano, Argentina decided to keep much of the rest of its surface fleet, including the carrier, closer to coastal waters or in ports for the rest of the war.
In the Persian Gulf six years later, the U.S. Navy’s ability to combine surveillance, aircraft, ships, and precision weapons devastated Iranian naval forces during Operation Praying Mantis. In a single day, U.S. forces sank or badly damaged several Iranian surface vessels operating in the confined waters of the Gulf, including two large frigates. Whereas the Falklands War illustrated the political consequences of losing a major warship, Praying Mantis highlighted the danger for ships facing an adversary with a much more effective “kill chain”—the sensors and communications to detect, identify, track, target, and attack an opponent’s fleet. For Taiwan, the lesson is that the combat power of large warships is irrelevant if they cannot survive long enough to fight, and an early loss could have cascading effects on the navy’s sustained combat operations.
Losing a smaller ship is less costly politically and militarily than losing a larger warship. In 2006, for instance, a Hezbollah cruise missile struck the Israeli corvette Hanit, which was operating in the waters off Lebanon. The ship had not been warned of the threat and had little time to detect and respond to a missile launched from shore 12 miles away, and some of its defensive systems were not fully activated. The missile killed four sailors and damaged the ship’s equipment, but the crew contained the damage and the Hanit limped home. The attack did not lead Israel to abandon corvettes; instead, it built larger, better-armed corvettes.
Most important for Taiwan, Ukraine’s Black Sea campaign after Russia’s invasion in 2022 showed that a weaker power can constrain a stronger one in contested waters without commanding the sea or possessing a comparable fleet. The campaign combined land-based antiship cruise missiles, swarms of uncrewed surface vessels, aerial drones, and external intelligence to impose heavy costs on Russian naval operations in the Black Sea. These attacks helped push much of Russia’s fleet farther from Ukraine’s shores. The sinking of the flagship Moskva, for example, showed that even a ship equipped with layered air defenses was vulnerable to an adversary’s kill chain. The ongoing war in Iran reinforces this pattern: the United States and Israel severely damaged Iran’s surface navy early in the conflict, but they have had difficulty eliminating dispersed missiles, drones, patrol craft and mine-laying boats. The result is that Iran, despite losing much of its conventional naval power, has retained the ability to threaten shipping and disrupt access to the Strait of Hormuz.
As these examples show, a less powerful navy does not need to control its coastal waters to deny a stronger adversary the ability to use them. In the Taiwan Strait, therefore, the goal should be “sea denial”: preventing China from using the waterway freely enough to carry out an invasion. Achieving sea denial does not require Taiwan to abandon its surface navy. But it must build a different kind of fleet—one based on a greater number of smaller ships that can operate independently while sharing information and coordinating their attacks, making the fleet more likely to survive an initial assault and repel an invasion force.
Finland and Sweden are good models. Both countries must deter and defend against a larger, more powerful adversary—Russia—and they are simultaneously contesting sovereignty challenges to areas they control and preparing for potential amphibious attacks on their coasts. With navies built around corvette-class-sized ships, Finland and Sweden have successfully stood up to Russian pressure, harassing Russian submarines that have violated their territorial seas. They have escorted away Russian ships that entered their waters and lodged diplomatic protests with Moscow. Both countries have extensive, sophisticated, and steadily improving surveillance, communications, and decision-support networks.
A restructuring of Taiwan’s surface fleet is within reach. In July, Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te attended the commissioning ceremony of the navy’s eighth and newest missile patrol ship—a lightweight but heavily armed corvette built in Taiwan with an innovative catamaran hull that makes the ship faster and more stable—and four more of these vessels are scheduled to be commissioned by the end of the year. Taiwan’s shipbuilding industry can rapidly produce these vessels, and the more it builds, the more efficient it will become. Sustained production would bring costs down, and each successive batch of vessels can incorporate new weapons, sensors, and uncrewed systems as they develop. Each of these ships has been delivered to the navy for less than $200 million, whereas a single 7,000-ton warship will cost an estimated $2 billion.
These changes should be combined with a broader upgrading of Taiwan’s armed forces’ network of sensors, communications tools, drones, and missiles. Taiwan is already making some of these investments. Its most recent special budget and the next round of its naval plans strengthen the kill chain with maritime surveillance drones, upgraded command-and-control networks to direct and coordinate military forces, and artificial intelligence–assisted combat decision support systems. These are the essential building blocks of an effective system to deny China the ability to freely navigate the Taiwan Strait. But the same technologies that make Taiwan’s kill chain more effective also make its large surface ships susceptible to attacks. Only by restructuring and upgrading its surface fleet can Taiwan be ready for a potential invasion.
A restructured Taiwanese surface fleet would also support plans to build eight new submarines, the first of which is already in sea trials. Submarines are slower but stealthier than corvettes. Missiles and drones launched from corvettes can disable ships by hitting them above the surface, and torpedoes launched from submarines can sink them. Changing its approach to its surface fleet is a key part of how Taiwan can make its other naval investments more effective.
The obstacles to the transformation of Taiwan’s navy are more institutional than technical. Because they are highly visible, large ships are attractive to politicians. They bring contracts for shipyards, ribbon-cutting ceremonies, a sense of national achievement, and visible proof of the government’s commitment to national security. By contrast, the public cannot see a warehouse full of drones or a mobile missile launcher hidden in the mountains. For navy leadership, too, the status quo is easier than pushing for major change. Taiwan’s destroyers and frigates, many of which are based on 50-year-old American designs, are well understood and therefore institutionally safe choices.
But rather than continue to upgrade these obsolescent, if not obsolete, ships, Taiwan should progressively decommission them and redirect scarce resources toward the lighter surface ships it needs. Moving away from familiar platforms will require political and military leaders to take risks and overcome the setbacks and criticism that accompany any institutional change. Production of Taiwan’s first domestically built submarines, for instance, is currently behind schedule. But such challenges are inevitable when dealing with complex vessels and should not derail necessary investments. Government and defense leaders need to sustain support for these programs and justify their importance to the public, even when opposition politicians criticize them.
After years of stagnation and decline, Taiwan’s defense spending is finally increasing. Taiwan’s proposed 2027 defense budget is likely to surpass three percent of GDP, and the legislature also passed a $25 billion special defense budget in May (a significant sum, albeit down from the $40 billion originally proposed by the executive branch). But Taiwan will not be more secure if these resources are spent on outdated defense concepts and a small number of vulnerable large warships. The country needs a dispersed, agile, and lethal force structure to defeat China in the Taiwan Strait. Such a navy will not look as impressive during a fleet review, but it will be a more effective deterrent against a potential Chinese invasion.
articles.summary: A nimbler navy can deny China.

articles.title: The Case for a Stalemate With Iran
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
JAMES F. JEFFREY is Philip Solondz Distinguished Fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. He served as a Foreign Service officer in seven U.S. administrations. From 2018 to 2020, he was Special Representative for Syria Engagement and Special Envoy to the Global Coalition to Defeat ISIS.
Six months in, the U.S. and Israeli war on Iran has settled into a stalemate. Neither Washington nor Tehran can achieve a clear military or diplomatic victory. Instead, the two sides have found themselves locked in a mutual blockade of oil and other shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and into Iranian ports, with no obvious way to change the status quo. The costs of accommodating the other side’s demands to end the stalemate are so high, and the costs of the stalemate sufficiently low, that a mutual blockade has emerged as the least bad option for both the United States and Iran for the foreseeable future.
This situation may not be ideal for Washington, but it avoids both defeat and escalation. It also works to the United States’ advantage over time: as the blockade drags on, Tehran’s position is likely to weaken faster than Washington’s. The United States has its own ample oil supplies to draw from, whereas nearly the entirety of Iran’s oil exports—and therefore much of its hard currency—has been cut off. An ongoing blockade that gradually ratchets up pressure on Iran could make Tehran more flexible in negotiations with the United States, leading to a compromise that Washington could accept. The challenge is to ensure that Tehran does not choose to respond to its worsening position by escalating its attacks and starting another regionwide conflict that ensnares the United States.
U.S. policy should focus on avoiding the most disruptive contingencies, especially Iranian escalation, and settle for maintaining dual blockades indefinitely. If Iran is unwilling to concede, Washington can slowly erode the Iranian economy and military while ensuring that Tehran cannot rebuild the strong regional position it enjoyed before the Hamas attack on Israel on October 7, 2023. At this stage, maintaining the current U.S. position is the most effective way of fighting—and winning—this war.
In June, Washington and Tehran agreed to a memorandum of understanding to first establish a cease-fire and open the Strait of Hormuz and then to sign a permanent deal within 60 days to resolve long-term issues in the bilateral relationship, including restricting Iran’s nuclear program and removing U.S. and international sanctions and other financial penalties on Iran. But it fell apart before a final deal could be reached largely because Iran failed to fully open the strait. With diplomatic solutions going nowhere, both Washington and Tehran are now hoping that the economic pressure each can put on the other—and in the case of Iran, on the global economy—will force its counterpart back to the negotiating table on terms that will resolve the blockade in its favor.
A blockade comes with costs for Washington. Keeping the strait closed is raising gas prices and increasing inflation in the United States, an especially sensitive issue as the November midterm elections approach. Prices could rise further if Iran finds a way to limit the millions of barrels of oil that bypass its blockade and are transported through the Strait of Hormuz daily. And the United States has already used up many critical munitions and strained its troops in the region by keeping the war going.
But the operation has been relatively affordable compared with past conflicts. The United States lost thousands of lives and spent trillions of dollars in Afghanistan and Iraq, whereas the ongoing conflict with Iran has resulted in 18 American service members killed and has likely cost tens of billions of dollars. (As of mid-July, estimates ranged from $37.5 billion to over $100 billion.) Most important, the mutual blockade has the advantage of being more palatable to political leaders in Washington than any of the alternative options.
A full U.S. withdrawal from the Strait of Hormuz without gaining concessions from Iran, including ending its blockade, would be unthinkable even for the unorthodox Trump administration. It would allow Iran to tout a complete victory and give the regime in Tehran a powerful psychological boost that would undo much of the progress that the United States and Israel made in the past three years decimating Iran’s network of regional proxies. And it would probably not lead Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz for free passage—Tehran is likely to insist on installing some kind of tolling system in perpetuity. With Washington in retreat, Iran could also revive and rebuild its nuclear program, which would be a stunning failure for the United States.
Military escalation is an even less appealing option for Washington. The Iranian regime has already survived a massive bombing campaign; a new, even more aggressive offensive could take out much of Iran’s remaining military capabilities and its energy, transportation, and communications infrastructure, but such an offensive could not guarantee that Tehran would accept American terms on opening the strait or curtailing its nuclear program. Having already weathered so many attacks aimed at diminishing its power, the remaining Iranian leadership, which learned to tolerate hardship in the Iran-Iraq War in the 1980s, is unlikely to be cowed by further aggression. Moreover, it could retaliate by targeting Gulf Arab states’ infrastructure and depleting remaining U.S. air defense missiles, which would raise the costs of the war to the United States and its partners.
The other option for the United States is a land invasion aimed at forcibly ousting the Iranian regime. This would require a military effort likely as large as the 1991 Desert Storm operation, which involved more than 500,000 American troops. Such an operation risks the significant loss of American life, huge costs to Iranian civilians, and disorder across the entire region. The Trump administration, which has consistently derided prior U.S. “forever wars” in the Middle East, appears to have ruled this option out months ago.
Washington’s calculation, then, is that a blockade is preferable to any other alternative. The blockade serves as a slow-moving pressure campaign either to bring Iran back to the negotiating table to agree to something along the lines of the compromise outlined in the June memorandum of understanding or to gradually weaken the Islamic Republic’s economic and military strength and eventually its internal stability. This type of campaign has a mixed historical record, but it worked in 1988 when, after eight years of war with Iraq and a failed naval confrontation with the United States in the Persian Gulf, Iran ended hostilities by withdrawing its troops from Iraq.
So far, the costs of the mutual blockade have been tolerable for the United States. Despite six months of an almost continuous Gulf oil and natural gas embargo by Iran, the global economy is suffering minimal damage. In July, five months into the war, the International Monetary Fund revised its 2026 global GDP growth estimates downward only 0.1 percentage point—from 3.1 percent to 3.0 percent—“with limited evidence of second round effects” of the oil shock. American gasoline prices have risen about 38 percent over the course of the war, but the country’s economic growth rate remains steady. Deeper shortages could push gas prices higher, but because the United States now produces more oil than it consumes, Washington could intervene in the market to keep prices down. In this context, the United States can continue the mutual blockade at relatively low cost.
The leaders of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps have held on to power so far—and seem poised to stay in power indefinitely. They have shifted Iran to a crisis economy, tightening their grip on the population and protecting their military programs at the expense of the Iranian people. They do not want to concede to terms like those in the memorandum of understanding because doing so would cost them their last major weapon—the ability to close the strait—and make them face possible new restrictions on their nuclear program. (In the June memorandum, for example, Tehran only vaguely committed to dilute its highly enriched uranium, which is Washington’s priority in reducing the Iranian nuclear threat.)
The United States, however, has time on its side. If Washington maintains its blockade through November’s election, the strategic value of the closure to Iran will decline as flights and tourist travel drop from summer highs and as countries improve their coping strategies by finding alternative energy suppliers. And in Iran, the effects of the blockade on its oil exports are already being felt. Inflation rose to over 80 percent year-over-year in August, and the value of the currency has been dropping rapidly. Iran’s leadership may be hardened by war, but the country’s economy will eventually need oil exports and reduced sanctions to survive. The economic pressure has pushed some political leaders, including President Masoud Pezeshkian, to suggest a return to the terms of the memorandum of understanding with the United States.
But if the pressure on the economy makes Tehran desperate, Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps leaders who ultimately call the shots could choose to escalate the situation rather than seek compromise. Iran could crack down further on any U.S. efforts to squeeze ships through the strait, including by laying new mines (as it was preparing to do on August 30, prompting a U.S. strike), and it could attempt to shut down Saudi and Emirati pipelines that bypass the strait and channel millions of barrels of oil daily from the Gulf. Alternatively, in addition to its current sporadic attacks, Tehran could launch a major military offensive, using its remaining stocks of missiles and drones to destroy much of the Gulf Arab states’ infrastructure, damage U.S. bases and ships, and even strike Israel. If such an attack succeeds, Gulf Arab states’ need to save their huge oil infrastructure investments could knock them out of their informal American coalition or force Washington to accept Iranian terms on reopening the strait.
If Iran escalated in this way, the Trump administration would have to retaliate militarily despite its reluctance to do so. According to foreign military sources, the United States and Israel had planned just such a massive air offensive in early August that would have been far larger and more damaging than earlier bombings. But Washington canceled the attack in part because of Gulf Arab states’ concerns about potential retaliation.
Any of the scenarios is possible. Iran has traditionally chosen to escalate, but given how hard its economy and its proxies have been hit since 2023, it is possible that it is willing to negotiate rather than surrender. As the stalemate drags on, and if Washington does not budge, Iran’s leadership thus will eventually have to decide which of the three available options it wants to pursue: negotiating a compromise similar to the memorandum of understanding, raising the stakes with aggressive action, or prolonging the blockade while finding itself in an increasingly disadvantageous position.
When the United States and Israel launched their attack on Iran in February, they could not foresee that six months later the result would be a double blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. Israeli and American leaders likely thought they would have destroyed the regime or forced Tehran to compromise. But now, given the alternatives, embracing the stalemate is the best possible option for the United States. The United States was unable to quickly defeat Iran, but it remains better able to absorb the costs of the current blockade as Iran’s economy slowly buckles under the strain.
The biggest risk to an ongoing stalemate is if Iran decides to escalate. Washington needs to warn Iran of the severe consequences it would face if it were to launch a large offensive or restart its nuclear program. Only American power can deter Iran. Washington thus should play to a stalemate but be ready to respond with a truly devastating counteroffensive if Iran raises the stakes. With the U.S. position getting stronger over time, Iran’s only real advantages lie in pushing back just enough to avoid triggering such a U.S. response.
A stalemate accompanied by the right threats can be a strategy for not only winning the war but also for solidifying and building on the essential gains Washington has made in its larger three-year conflict with Iran and its proxies. It will not transform the Middle East on its own, but by putting Iran in a weaker position, it could encourage much-needed restraint from Tehran.
articles.summary: America can win if it stays the course.

articles.title: The End of American Sanctuary
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
SETH G. JONES is President of the Defense and Security Department at the Center for Strategic and International Studies and the author of The American Edge: The Military Tech Nexus and the Sources of Great Power Dominance.
Among its many advantages, the United States benefits from a rare form of geographic luck: it is bracketed on the east and west by two vast moats, the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, and on the north and south by only two neighbors, both of whom are relatively friendly. Adding to this good fortune is that, since the end of World War II, the United States has possessed a powerful nuclear arsenal and unparalleled military, economic, and technological might. Despite the 9/11 terrorist attacks, this mix of geography, deterrence, and power has led many Americans to feel almost untouchable at home. According to a 2024 Chicago Council on Global Affairs poll, just 19 percent of those surveyed expressed concern about foreign threats.
It is time for Americans to revise their assumptions. In fact, the U.S. homeland has never been as vulnerable to attack as it is today. China, Russia, and North Korea are building up their conventional and nuclear capabilities to strike the United States across a variety of domains—and U.S. defenses have not kept pace. A major evolution in technology and tactics, meanwhile, has increased the threat of subversion and gray-zone attacks: drones from state and nonstate actors can strike almost any target in the United States, and adversaries such as China can conduct AI-enabled offensive cyber-operations that can destroy or damage critical infrastructure.
The United States is not prepared. The country’s air and missile defenses are porous. Arcane domestic laws and policies prevent the necessary coordination and authority to defend against drone attacks. And energy, water, financial, health-care, and other infrastructure remain vulnerable to advanced cyberattacks. Faced with these new threats, federal, state, and local entities in the United States are caught flat-footed. The 9/11 attacks happened in part because of policymakers’ inability to grasp that the world was changing and to share information across government agencies that could have protected the country. Without an overhaul of the nation’s homeland security apparatus, Washington is in danger of making this mistake again.
Security measures enacted after September 11 were designed to protect the U.S. homeland from terrorism. The U.S.A. Patriot Act and subsequent legislation enabled U.S. agencies to collect more intelligence at home and abroad. The Department of Homeland Security, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, the National Counterterrorism Center, and the Joint Terrorism Task Forces were created or enhanced to better share intelligence about terrorism and other threats. The FBI significantly expanded the number of Joint Terrorism Task Forces across the country, coordinated with state and local law enforcement, and conducted intelligence-led operations to identify and arrest terrorists.
These measures were helpful at the time, when terrorism was the biggest threat to the U.S. homeland. And they were successful in preventing the vast majority of terrorist plots in the homeland. But today, some of the greatest threats to the United States come from state actors. China, Russia, and North Korea all possess intercontinental missiles capable of hitting the U.S. homeland—and all have conducted tests and exercises to show that they are capable of using them.
The wars in Iran and Ukraine suggest that possessing a nuclear arsenal, even one as large as the U.S. arsenal, no longer protects against conventional attacks on the homeland as it once did. Iran and its network of proxy forces have lobbed tens of thousands of rockets, missiles, and drones at major population centers in Israel. Ukraine has successfully struck Russian cities, energy infrastructure, industrial base targets, logistics nodes, and military bases without incurring a nuclear response from the Kremlin. Advanced Israeli and Russian air and missile defense systems have struggled to stop these drones and missile attacks.
In the event of a conventional attack on U.S. soil, American air and missile defense systems might, too. The United States lacks sufficient numbers of air defense systems and interceptors to protect against ballistic missiles. The war with Iran has reduced the military’s global supply of THAAD interceptors by as much as 80 percent and Patriot interceptors by as much as 50 percent. In addition, homeland defense against cruise missiles remains porous. Cruise missiles are difficult to defend against. They fly close to the earth in order to stay below conventional radar, and they use mountains, valleys, and hills to hide from ground-based sensors—what is called “terrain masking.” The United States does not have enough missile defense systems in enough areas to protect against cruise missiles.
China especially has expanded and updated its ability to strike the United States. In addition to missiles, the threat from China now extends into space. China can strike targets in the U.S. homeland using a Fractional Orbital Bombardment System, which places a warhead flying at hypersonic speed into low-earth orbit, allowing it to approach the U.S. homeland from an unpredictable direction and bypass traditional early warning radar and missile defense networks. The People’s Liberation Army is also researching other space-based capabilities, such as orbital strike weapons, which would theoretically strike the U.S. homeland by dropping projectiles from space.
The U.S. homeland is also facing novel subversion threats. State and nonstate actors have long used physical sabotage against critical infrastructure, disinformation, and offensive cyber-operations to weaken their adversaries below the threshold of conventional warfare. But new technologies and tactics, including AI, present new challenges for the United States.
Drones are the most obvious example. Technological advances have already made drones cheaply and readily available for purchase, with longer ranges, higher payloads, and an improved ability to evade electronic warfare. Adversaries may soon be able to fly drones in coordinated swarms using AI, effectively overwhelming any defenses. Allies and adversaries alike are now engaged in an arms race, ramping up drone production and use in an attempt to innovate their way to the cutting edge. Russia is producing as many as seven million weaponized drones per year. According to some estimates, China has the capacity to build one billion drones per year.
It wouldn’t take that much, however, to wreak havoc on the U.S. homeland. In 2025, Ukraine smuggled over 100 drones into Russia inside cargo trucks to conduct strikes that damaged or destroyed roughly one-third of Russia’s active bomber fleet and caused approximately $7 billion in damages. Operation Spider’s Web was a spectacular success for Ukrainian forces—and a chilling reminder of the United States’ susceptibility to a similar attack. An adversary could conceal weaponized drones inside modified cargo vans, shipping containers, or trucks with slidable roofs and position the vehicles near high-value targets, such as military airfields or naval bases, without detection. They could program the drones to launch simultaneously using commercial cellular networks, circumventing domestic air defense and signal-jamming measures and effectively bypassing strategic early warning radar systems.
Such an attack on U.S. soil might seem far-fetched. But unauthorized drone incursions on U.S. military installations, nuclear power plants, and other critical infrastructure—not to mention outdoor concert venues, sports stadiums, transportation infrastructure, and ports—have been increasing over the past several years. In March, for example, Barksdale Air Force Base in Louisiana, which houses long-range B-52 bombers, went into lockdown after numerous unauthorized drones were spotted hovering over sensitive areas of the base. In June, the FBI arrested five suspects in an alleged plot to target the Ultimate Fighting Championship event on the White House South Lawn with explosive-laden drones. Artificial intelligence makes individual drones and swarms of drones harder to stop because they do not rely on remote radio signals that can be jammed by electronic countermeasures.
Drones are not the only problem made worse by AI’s rapid development. Agentic AI systems such as Anthropic’s Mythos will make it far easier for state and nonstate adversaries, such as terrorists, to penetrate cyberdefenses and attack critical infrastructure at a scale never before possible. Once directed, AI agents can discover flaws in corporate and government computer systems and execute self-directed cyberattacks with minimal human oversight. Even before the advent of these AI systems, the shockingly poor state of national and municipal cyberdefenses made American critical infrastructure an inviting target. Beginning in 2021, China’s Volt Typhoon attacks infiltrated U.S. power grids, water treatment plants, telecommunication systems, and transportation hubs, embedding malware that could sabotage them in the event of a U.S.-Chinese crisis. An AI-enabled Volt Typhoon operation would allow attackers to shift from a slow, human-enabled campaign that takes months or years to a nearly instantaneous, self-adapting campaign against numerous targets simultaneously that could be vastly more damaging.
Finally, beyond drones and AI, there is the growing threat of direct-ascent antisatellite weapons, which are missiles launched from the ground, sea, or air that travel into space to strike and destroy a satellite in orbit, as well as directed-energy weapons and electronic warfare systems that can target U.S. satellites in low-earth orbit and geosynchronous orbit. China and Russia are actively developing and testing a broad range of antisatellite and other counterspace weapons. If implemented, such space-based attacks could degrade GPS and navigation, ground commercial flights, and disrupt logistics networks that rely on satellite tracking for freight. In other words, they could at least temporarily grind daily life in the United States to a halt.
To better prepare for an attack on the homeland, Washington needs first to fortify the active defenses that protect the country’s critical infrastructure. It needs to build and deploy more upper-range systems like Patriot and THAAD for ballistic missiles, medium-range systems such as the Indirect Fire Protection Capability system for cruise missiles, and short-range systems such as the Coyote and Merops systems to counter drones. Directed-energy weapons—such as high-energy lasers and high-power microwave systems—and radio-frequency jamming and electronic warfare systems are also useful to defend against drone attacks. The United States needs more systems to defend critical infrastructure, as well as training for personnel. It should also ramp up passive defenses, such as digging underground facilities for vital infrastructure and placing high-density and layered concrete barriers around ground systems, power-generation units, ammunition storage facilities, and barracks.
Since it would be exorbitantly expensive to protect everything in the homeland, Washington should initially focus on reinforcing critical bases and infrastructure that China or other adversaries could target in a conflict. Key locations include military command-and-control facilities, bomber bases, nuclear weapons sites, air and missile defense systems, and major naval bases.
Golden Dome, the Trump administration’s proposed homeland air and missile defense system, can play an important role in this effort. The plan aims to create a unified command-and-control network of sensors, weapons, and other systems to detect and shoot down incoming drones and missiles. But Golden Dome is underfunded and has been slow to get off the ground. Moving forward, the U.S. priority should be accelerating plans to stitch together existing capabilities—not developing new ones—such as the U.S. military’s missile warning satellites; global network of radars and sensors; 44 ground-based interceptors in California and Alaska; and other federal, state, local, and commercial systems. The U.S. military also needs to ramp up live-fire exercises to test Golden Dome’s software and ability to detect, track, and hit incoming threats.
Drones present a thornier problem. Commanders at military bases and personnel protecting critical infrastructure often do not have the legal authority to destroy or degrade drones that illegally fly into their airspace. Some recent laws, including the Safer Skies Act of 2025, grant state and local agencies (though not private-sector entities) greater license to detect and track hostile drones. But more comprehensive legislation is needed that allows operators who have received training to deploy and use counterdrone systems under federal or state and local law enforcement supervision. To mitigate the risk that newly empowered operators of counterdrone systems accidentally jam or shoot down civilian aircraft, more state and local personnel should be trained at the National Counter-UAS Training Center in Huntsville, Alabama.
Intelligence sharing among federal, state, and local intelligence agencies improved after 9/11 to disrupt terrorist networks and foil planned attacks. But the evolving nuclear and conventional capabilities of China, Russia, and North Korea, as well as emerging tactics and technology such as drones and AI, make the intelligence practices of the “war on terror” largely obsolete. What’s more, self-inflicted wounds have damaged the few agencies well suited for today’s threats. The Trump administration, for example, has gutted the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which oversees cyberdefenses and elections security. The United States needs to establish a robust National Counterintelligence Center, much like the National Counterterrorism Center it established after 9/11, that brings together analysts from multiple agencies to fuse intelligence, analyze threats, and coordinate strategic planning against Chinese, Iranian, Russian, and other threats to the homeland. At the state and local level, the Joint Terrorism Task Forces and Fusion Centers need to shift their focus and resources to tracking state-based threats to the homeland.
Finally, the threats currently facing the U.S. homeland require a fundamental shift in mindset. U.S. policymakers, the country’s security establishment, and its citizens must recognize that the United States is in a new era; it can no longer rely on its geography and its nuclear arsenal to protect it. Finland, Israel, and Ukraine have long traditions of developing strategic plans and communicating to their publics about homeland threats. The United States should follow suit by educating the American public about the evolving threats to the homeland and developing a national resilience plan—much as Finland has done—to harden critical infrastructure, closely collaborate with the private sector, adapt laws, and communicate with the public.
Americans’ overwhelming sense of safety was briefly and tragically shaken by the attacks on September 11, 2001, and the 9/11 Commission went on to argue that the United States faced a “generational challenge” from terrorist groups. A quarter century later, there is a new generation of Americans and a new generational challenge. If the 9/11 attacks were in large measure a failure of imagination and implementation, as the commission wrote, Washington risks repeating that same mistake today.
articles.summary: New threats demand a new homeland defense.

articles.title: How Does the World Really View China?
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
ADAM Y. LIU is an Assistant Professor at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy at the National University of Singapore.
In July, the Pew Research Center found that for the first time in roughly two decades of global polling, the world now views China more favorably than the United States. The sentiment was not universal, but in 25 of the 36 countries surveyed this year, the percentage of respondents who gave favorable marks to China exceeded that for the United States, including several close U.S. allies. Some analysts have taken these findings as confirmation that the golden era of American soft power is over and China is ascendant. According to them, Trump’s policies on tariffs, aid, and allies have eroded the United States’ standing, opening the door for people across the world to switch their allegiance to China.
But this interpretation, convenient as it may be, deserves more scrutiny. A closer examination of the data reveals that although global opinion of the United States has indeed plummeted and opinion of China has risen since 2022, most of the world still prefers the United States as an economic partner—including most of the countries that now view China in a more positive light. This is a critical distinction, since economic partnerships and interests tend to drive national policies. Indeed, it signals something more nuanced is happening than simply the end of American hegemony and an imminent age of Chinese global supremacy.
The world’s increasingly pro-Chinese attitude is not meaningless. That more and more people think better of Beijing than of Washington could eventually prove important as Beijing seeks to build up its soft power. For now, however, what the numbers actually show is a world adjusting to the new reality of great-power competition, feeling forced to choose one side without the luxury of liking it.
Favorability is, in essence, a feeling. When people are asked to say how favorably they view something, they are really being asked whether and how much they like it—and little else. Pew’s favorability question also asked only whether respondents hold a positive or a negative impression of China and the United States, not whether they liked one more than the other. Still, Beijing clearly came out on top in these questions. Favorable views of the United States fell significantly in 15 of the 24 countries surveyed in both 2025 and 2026. Moreover, in several U.S. ally countries, including Canada, France, Germany, Italy, South Korea, and the United Kingdom, favorability ratings are now at or near their lowest since Pew began polling in 2002. In contrast, China’s image has consistently improved in several Western countries. The percentage of Italian respondents with a favorable opinion of China, for instance, increased from 31 percent in 2022 to 51 percent in 2026. In Spain, China’s favorability rose from 37 percent in 2025 to 54 percent in 2026.
Media outlets and observers have fixated on these numbers, but the same Pew survey asks another, more consequential question: “Is it more important for your country to have strong economic ties with China or with the United States?” This prompt forces respondents to weigh the two powers against each other and pick one. Critically, it asks them to consider not just how they feel about each country but also which they would rather work with. In 2025, the last year for which country-by-country, individual-level data is available, more respondents in 20 out of 24 countries chose economic ties with the United States over ties with China.
In seven of those 20 countries, answers to the two questions diverged. More respondents in Canada, France, Greece, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, and Turkey rated China more favorably than the United States, yet more people chose economic ties with the United States over China, sometimes by wide margins. In Sweden, for example, respondents preferred U.S. economic ties to Chinese economic ties by 48 percentage points. Turkish respondents rated China 13 percentage points more favorably than they did the United States but preferred economic ties with the United States by ten percentage points anyway.
As the only country that favors Chinese economic ties but views the United States more favorably, Australia is an outlier. This is not much of a surprise given that China is already the country’s largest export destination, accounting for 30 percent of everything Australia sells to the world. But it is noteworthy that half of Australians believe China is the country that threatens Australia most, and a full third believe the United States is Australia’s most important ally, compared with seven percent who believe China is. When asked, however, whether Australia’s economy should have closer ties to China or to the United States, 54 percent picked China, compared with 43 percent that picked the United States. Favorability, it appears, cannot adequately capture the nuance of public opinion on the two countries, much less divine a shift in the balance of soft power.
Globally, the individual respondents who preferred China as an economic partner seem to have done so because they believe that China is already the world’s leading economic power. Sixty percent of global respondents who preferred economic ties with China believed as much, compared with 20 percent who think the United States is the world’s leading economic power. The same pattern holds true for the United States: roughly 58 percent of the people who prefer economic ties with the United States think that it is the global economic hegemon, whereas 26 percent believe that China is. This makes intuitive sense: people want to partner with whoever they think is the winner. But Pew’s data also suggests that people still have a desire to partner with Washington on economic matters, because many still say they want to even when they don’t think it is the winner. Of those who believe the United States still leads the world economy, 75 percent chose economic ties with the United States, compared with just 15 percent who chose a closer economic relationship with China. Yet among those who believe China has taken the lead, 49 percent chose China and a remarkable 38 percent still chose the United States.
Not everyone feels compelled to choose between the United States and China. Across the 24 countries surveyed in 2025, roughly one in nine respondents preferred that their country maintain strong economic ties with both powers rather than supporting one over the other. In some countries, this group of fence sitters is too large to ignore. Thirty-nine percent of Nigerians—a plurality of respondents—declined to choose between Washington and Beijing. So did 32 percent of Israelis, 27 percent of Hungarians, 23 percent of Germans, and 20 percent of Turks. Across all countries, 16 percent of those who named the United States as their country’s most important ally but believed China now leads the world economy opted not to choose a single most important economic partner, compared with 11 percent of all other respondents.
That is not to say that fence-sitting publics will remain undecided as the U.S.-Chinese competition intensifies. They may yet be moved to commit to a side if it looks like a reliable protector against a clear danger. For Washington, this is still good news. In 20 of the 24 countries surveyed, more people named the United States than China as their country’s most important ally. China leads in only Indonesia, Nigeria, South Africa, and Turkey. In no country did a majority name China, whereas the United States won majorities in five countries. That gap is Beijing’s weakness and Washington’s remaining advantage.
The Trump administration’s wavering commitment to allies threatens to undermine it. So might the common—and incorrect—belief that China has already won the economic race. By most measures, the U.S. economy is still the world’s largest and most productive. Yet in the eyes of the rest of the world, every new trade war and every rupture with an ally risks reinforcing the belief that the U.S. economy is headed in the wrong direction.
For now, however, fears that public opinion has tilted toward China are overblown. When forced to choose, most of the world still prefers working with Washington, and most of those who choose Beijing are likely betting on predictions about its economic rise. Beijing, then, should not mistake favorability for partnership. And Washington must keep the United States’ markets open and its commitments credible before the belief that the country’s economic future is behind it becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy.
articles.summary: The trouble with overestimating Beijing’s soft power.

articles.title: Can Israel End Its Forever Wars?
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
AMOS HAREL is Defense Analyst for Haaretz and the author of Anatomy of a Failure: The Road to October 7, which will be published in English in 2027.
As he prepares to face Israeli voters next month after three years of incessant war, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has formulated a new strategy. Ignoring the huge costs in blood and treasure, let alone in support for Israel in the United States and elsewhere, he now publicly and explicitly supports waging wars without end. As a lesson of Hamas’s October 7, 2023, massacre, he asserts that Israel needs to take preemptive military action against every potential security threat it faces, regardless of the consequences. This has left many wondering how much of this hard-line approach might change if Gadi Eisenkot, the veteran military official who is running ahead of Netanyahu in the polls, manages to defeat him.
Thus far, Eisenkot, a classic centrist, has been blunt and sometimes caustic in making the case against the prime minister. But apart from vague statements about ending the longest war in Israeli history, he has generally avoided going into detail about his own national security strategy. On some issues, such as dealing with Hamas in Gaza, he has sounded more hawkish than Netanyahu. And when he is asked about the future of the conflict with the Palestinians—Israel’s most politically explosive issue—he has been extremely careful to avoid binding commitments. In a rare statement on such matters in August, Eisenkot said he was opposed to a Palestinian state, endorsing what is by now a consensus position across Israel’s political center and even parts of the center left as well as the right.
From such statements, it might be tempting to conclude that an Eisenkot government would be little different from its right-wing predecessor. Indeed, some analysts have argued that there will be no real differences on major security issues at all. But that ignores a number of important areas, from the crisis in the West Bank to Israel’s approach to Syria to the conflict in Gaza, where new strategies could yield real dividends, even if the changes are most likely to be incremental rather than dramatic. The extent to which an opening emerges will depend greatly on U.S. President Donald Trump and the nature of his relationship with a post-Netanyahu government, if Israelis elect one. The most important question is not whether change is possible but what kinds of changes, and with what kinds of engagement from Washington.
According to Israeli polls, Netanyahu, chairman of the right-wing Likud Party, will find it extremely difficult to form a government after the October 27 elections. For now, he appears to be devoting most of his efforts to forcing a deadlock that would prevent his rivals from assembling the next coalition. At the same time, he has promoted his strategy of continuous war.
The new Netanyahu preaches zero concessions and zero compromises. To his domestic audience, he also emphasizes what he claims is another achievement: Israel’s seizure of territory on almost every border—in southern Lebanon, in Syria, in the Gaza Strip—as self-styled security zones. Defense Minister Israel Katz takes this approach one step further, claiming that Israel will remain in these zones for many years as part of the price it is exacting from its enemies. Katz and other ministers are constantly searching for new military foes: they have claimed that Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, who is deeply hostile to Israel but difficult to portray as a direct military antagonist, is now as much of a threat as Hezbollah and Hamas, an assertion that Netanyahu has also taken up. Some of these cabinet members have even maintained, without a shred of evidence, that Syria’s president, the former jihadist Ahmed al-Shara, is preparing to attack Israel.
This belligerent stance completely ignores the heavy price of the Netanyahu strategy. With large numbers of soldiers deployed on the forward fronts for months at a time, the Israel Defense Forces has had no time to train, and reservists are now bearing an enormous burden, serving on average more than 100 days a year since the 2023 attack. The Israeli economy has also taken an immense hit. According to the latest estimates, Israel has spent about $142 billion on the war since it began—equivalent to more than half of the country’s total annual budget. This is aside from the calamitous damage that the wars have wrought on Israel’s international reputation.
Amid these spiraling problems and the widespread unpopularity of the current right-wing coalition, Eisenkot has opened a substantial lead in the polls.
